title: Abhidhamma, closed
hook: mind, factors, matter, conditions, in plain words

segments.voice: Yesterday, an old monk who chose the sitting over the books, and nobody told him he was wrong. Your line: one way of looking. Did you let a grade go? Day one thousand ninety-six.

Back to the watchmaker's bench where this block began. Springs, gears, a tiny wheel, a jewel no bigger than a grain of sand, laid out on a cloth. Taken apart, it looks nothing like the thing on your wrist. And yet that's the only way to see how it keeps time. This block of the path did the same with a person. It laid a single moment open on the cloth and named the parts. Today the cloth gets folded up. The whole higher teaching, in plain words, before the path turns somewhere new.
screen: `BACK TO THE WATCHMAKER'S BENCH.` → `A MOMENT, LAID OPEN.` → `THE CLOTH FOLDED UP.`

segments.voice: First, where it sits. The Abhidhamma is the third basket of the Pali canon, seven books, from the list of mental states to the great book of conditions. Theravada tradition says the Buddha first taught it to his mother in a heaven, and in Myanmar it's still chanted for the dead and studied by lay people. Second, mind. Two ways of speaking: the everyday way, with people and tables, and the ultimate way, with moments. In the ultimate way, the mind is a stream of tiny moments, each one arising and passing. A mango falls on a sleeping man, and seeing it, smelling it, eating it, is a whole chain of those moments in a flash. Third, factors. Each moment is colored. Seven factors, the texts say, are in every moment: contact, feeling, perception and the rest. Then the troubled ones: restlessness, greed, conceit, envy, dullness, doubt. And the beautiful ones: mindfulness, conscience, calm, softness, compassion, gladness. Fourth, matter and conditions. Matter begins with the four great elements, earth, water, fire and air, and the body's own warmth and life. And nothing stands alone. The great book of relations traces how each thing holds up the next: roots, supports, friends, food, weather. Then the path widened the view. A book of debates with other schools. Another school's lists, counting differently. A mirror to sit with, a day of noticing, and a reminder that it's one way of looking, not a test. All of it from one idea: look closely enough, and what seemed solid turns out to be made of the smallest parts, each one arising, each one passing, each one leaning on the others.
screen: `THE THIRD BASKET, SEVEN BOOKS.` · `MIND: A STREAM OF MOMENTS.` · `FACTORS: TROUBLED AND BEAUTIFUL.` · then, large: `MATTER, AND EVERYTHING RELATES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: name one list you'll keep. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then let the lists from this block drift past, slowly, like cards turned over on a table. The seven in every moment. The troubled ones. The beautiful ones. The four great elements. The roots and supports. Don't sort them. Just notice which one your mind keeps coming back to. That's the one to keep. Say its name once, quietly, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Abhidhamma. The higher teaching: mind, factors, matter and conditions, the teaching broken down into its smallest parts. Today's word, and the close of this block.
Your line: the smallest parts. Today, take the one list you chose and use it once, out in the day. Tomorrow the path turns to the great vehicle. Day one thousand ninety-six.

howItsDone: Students of the Abhidhamma in Theravada countries may learn it from a short manual such as the Abhidhammattha Sangaha before turning to the seven books themselves, and some teachers use its lists alongside meditation.

myth: the Abhidhamma treats a person as one solid thing
it lays a moment open: a stream of mind-moments, colored by factors, leaning on conditions.
the Abhidhamma speaks in two ways, everyday and ultimate
people and tables in one, momentary mind and matter in the other.
in the Abhidhamma, things stand alone
the great book of relations traces how each thing holds up the next.

fork.setup: the block is over and the lists are spread out in front of you. what's the closing practice?
options: keep the one your mind returns to
put them all away for good
fork.reveal: name one list you'll keep, the one the mind keeps coming back to, and use it once out in the day.

original.note: Pali: the name of the third basket of the canon, which this path has called the higher teaching.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long, dry catalog.
what it means: one idea, looked at closely: what seems solid is made of small parts, arising, passing and leaning on each other.
what a scholar hears: the four ultimate realities, consciousness, mental factors, matter and nibbana, with the Patthana's conditions binding them, as the manuals arrange them.

notes: Block close (days 1062–1096): recaps the block's titles and carries without adding new claims; counts (seven books, seven universal factors, four great elements) come from the earlier days' sources.
Mango simile cited to the Atthasalini (the commentary on the Dhammasangani); day 1069 should carry the exact citation. Confirm.
'Abhidhamma' is glossed as 'the higher teaching' following day 1062's title, not as an etymology.
howItsDone: learning from the Abhidhammattha Sangaha first is common practice; 'often' could be softened to 'some'.
